newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan's Hashimoto crashes to earth in poll showing.
newsitem.headline: Japan's Hashimoto crashes to earth in poll showing.

text.p: A week is a long time in politics.

Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, who last week basked in the glow of parliament's smooth passage of his budget for fiscal 1997, has come down to earth after a major opinion poll revealed his cabinet's popularity is at a record low.

Support for the Hashimoto cabinet slumped to 36.1 percent in a weekend opinion poll, an 11 percentage point drop from a similar survey in January, taking his approval to the lowest level since he took office in January 1996, the Nihon Keizai Shimbun business daily said.
The percentage of respondents who said they did not support the administration was 37.5 percent, which exceeded the number of supporters.
Those surveyed cited "bad policies" and "Hashimoto's lack of leadership" as the main reasons for not supporting the prime minister, the newspaper said.
"Clearly the spear of criticism is pointed directly at the prime minister himself," the paper said in an analysis of the survey results.

Doubts about Hashimoto's leadership have grown along with public disappointment at the 1997 budget, in which he was unable to kill off bullet train lines and other pricey pet projects pushed by the Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) of which Hashimoto is president.

Echoing financial markets and economists, the moderate daily newspaper Mainichi Shimbun in a recent editorial blasted the budget as giving Japan's construction companies "a continuing pork-barrel paradise".
Hashimoto, arguably the most forceful politician to head Japan in a decade, had pledged his administration would cut bureaucracy and deal with rising public debt.

"The gap between expectations and reality was like an audience which applauded in anticipation of an energetic performance from a conductor, only to find that the conductor was merely playing along at the orchestra's pace," the newspaper's analysis said.

While about half the voters who said they supported the opposition expressed dissatisfaction with Hashimoto's commitment to fiscal reform, a similar number of LDP supporters said they also opposed the reforms.

Despite the conservative LDP's pro-business image, the party, which ruled Japan virtually unchallenged from 1955-93, is an umbrella that protects farmers, small shopkeepers and a host of other interest groups threatened by drastic reform.

The LDP, which from mid-1994 dominated a coalition with the Social Democratic Party and the tiny Sakigake Party, returned to sole power in Lower House elections last October, ruling as a minority government with those two parties' backing.

The Socialists and Sakigake gave Hashimoto's government the votes it needed to pass the 77.7 trillion yen ($642 billion) budget without paying heed to opposition calls for spending cuts and amendments.

But the two parties disagree with the LDP over how to deal with a festering dispute over U.S. bases on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, which will reach a critical phase in mid-May when leases for U.S. facilities expire.
A senior LDP official this week warned of an "April crisis" for Hashimoto if the parties cannot agree on a way to overcome Okinawa opposition to extend the leases.
But even as Hashimoto struggles with his LDP's pork-barrel image and testy partners, he faces no immediate threat from the major opposition parties.

Both the scandal-plagued Shinshinto (New Frontier Party) and the Democratic Party have been paralysed in recent weeks by leadership squabbles and failed to mount an effective challenge to the LDP, political analysts said.
